full_judgment: 9. Mr Md Shamsul Haque, learned Advocate for the plaintiff-opposite parties submits that the original deed dated 17-6-1967 was never produced before the Court or any other Authority for mutation, preparation of record-of-rights, payment of revenue etc. and there was no explanation in the written statement as to the where about of the original deed and evidences as regards the missing of the original deed have been apparently untrustworthy. No GD was lodged as regards the missing of the original title deed, even the certified copy of the said deed was taken back without any explanation and was submitted after a long time before this Court only after the police went to the suit-land for execution of the decree of Appellate Court below. The custody of the registered agreement for reconveyance dated 4-6-1966 in original in the hands of the plaintiff-opposite parties herein speaks against the execution of the deed dated 17-6-1967. When the agreement in original was filed in Court by the plaintiff, the defendant No. 1 could not legally satisfy the Court why the agreement in original was not handed over to the defendant No. 1 before registration of the deed dated 17-6-1967. The plaintiff's suit was for redemption of 15 decimal land but the defendants claimed 20 decimal on the strength of the deed dated 17-6-1967 which was straight way denied by the plaintiff, the defendant No. 1 did not prove his possession over the additional 5 decimal of land, no mutation, no record of rights, no payment of revenue of the defendant No. 1 was produced before the Court though the defendant No. 1 claimed that he purchased the said 15 + 05 = 20 decimal of land on 17-6-1967, so it is the conclusive circumstantial proof that the said deed dated 17-6-1967 being a forged deed was never produced by the defendant No. 1 and was never acted upon. Whereas the plaintiff has upto date record of right and up to date payment of revenue as regards the said additional 5 decimal of land, being his paternal property, is the conclusive proof of possession and title of the plaintiff-opposite parties. Mr Haque then submits that the so-called deed dated 17-6-1967 is ex facie a vague one as it does not mention specifically the value of the additional 5 decimals of land and the value of the right of reconveyance while both the instrument required separate stamp and registration cost specifically. Mr Haque further submits that the defendant in depositions and cross-examinations and also at paragraph No. 5 of his/their application for stay of the execution case filed before this Court on 1st day of July, 1998 clearly stated that he has transferred the suit-land to one Ambia Khatun on 17-4-1983 and 11-5-1983 and the plaintiff-opposite parties instituted the suit for redemption on 3-6-1983 and why the defendant No. 1 petitioners is/are fighting the legal battle without impleading said Ambia Khatun and why said Ambia Khatun is not coming for stay of the execution case ? Such contradictory claim and conduct of the defendant petitioners overwhelmingly proves his/their fraud and forgery and thus the plaintiff opposite parties has /have been deprived of the benefit of the suit-land for more than 4 decades. Mr Shamsul Haque then submits that as per section 6(h) of the Transfer of Property Act there can be no transfer to any disqualified transferee. The transferee of the alleged deed dated 17-6-1967 was already a transferee as regards 15 decimals of the suit land as per the registered deed dated 4-6-1966 and therefore he was a disqualified transferee in a deed dated 17-6-1967 where the said 15 decimals of land was in the schedule of both the deeds dated 4-6-1966 and 17-6-1967. The registration of the subsequent deed amounts to cancellation of the earlier deed which is not permitted in law and the sub-registrar was without lawful authority in registering the subsequent deed dated 17-6-1967 and similarly as per section 7 of the Transfer of Property Act only person entitled to transferable property is competent to transfer the said transferable property. While a validly registered deed dated 4-6-1966 was in force and was admitted by the parties, the transferor of the said deed dated 4-6-1966 was already a transferor in respect of 15 decimals of land and he could not be a valid transferor in the deed dated 17-6-1967 where in the schedule the said 15 decimals of land was included. The subsequent deed could not be registered and law cannot be changed by consent of the parties. The subsequent deed in the instant case was simply void, which even does not require a declaration that the said deed is void. Such a deed whenever is produced for any practical purpose would not be accepted and liable to be impounded by any lawful authority and as per section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act an ostensible owner can transfer any property. Now as per the deed dated 4-6-1966 the defendant was ostensible owner and the defendant could sell the suit land, then how a person entitled to sell could buy the same suit land from a person who is already a transferor and at the later time he had no title no interest in the suit land. Until his right to reconveyance was specifically enforced and the suit land was transferred back to him by a registered deed, he had no right, title and interest on 17-6-1967 over the suit land and he could not execute the subsequent deed as regards the 15 decimal of land. Mr Haque then submits that as per section 4 of the Stamp Act, 1899 additional stamp is required for additional instrument. Obviously the alleged deed dated 17-6-1967 had additional instrument, however no consideration was specified for the additional instrument, namely the right of reconveyance, and, as such, no separate stamp was used and no registration cost was paid and it was also not clear what was the consideration for the additional 5 decimals of land. As per section 14 there can be no second instrument on same stamp paper and section 15 of the said Act provides that such deed is deemed as unstamped which is liable to be impounded whenever it is produced, and sections 27, 33, 35, 43, 57, 61(4), 62, taken together the said deed was liable to be impounded, not admissible in evidence and the person in possessesion of such a deed is liable for criminal action as per the Stamp Act and then submits that as per Schedule 1(55) of the Stamp Act, 1999 the right of reconveyance could be released or renounced as per law upon payment of specified stamp duty but the defendant No. 1 had arranger for registration of a forged deed dated 17-6-1967 which was if registered at all was registered illegally and that is an invalid document which can never be acted upon and has been acted upon in the last about 50 years and as per the Registration Act once sale deed is registered, the same cannot be cancelled by consent or by subsequent deed (AIR 2011 Mad 66 FB), and a sale deed once registered can be avoided only by a subsequent registered document transfer (27 CWN 8 PC) and then submits that as per section 95A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act read with the decisions reported in 34 DLR (AD) 237, 66 DLR (AD) 162, 20 BLC (AD) 4 the plaintiff-opposite party is entitled to recover possession of the 15 decimal of the suit land. Mr Haque then submits the plaintiffs case stands proved by admission of the defendant No. 1 and the defendant's case being denied by the plaintiff, the Evidence Act provides onus upon the defendant to prove his case, because in the absence of any evidence in this case the plaintiff is entitled to the decree in his favour inasmuch as the plaintiffs case has been admitted by the defendant and the plaintiff acquired title by operation of law and the Appellate Court below findings as regards burden of proof is in accordance with law and the trial Court erred in law as regards onus of proof and thus the Rule is liable to be discharged. In support of his contentions he has referred to the case of Emmanuele Grech vs Antonio Grech, reported in 6 DLR 599 case of Haji Waziullah vs Additional Deputy Commissioner, reported in 41 DLR 96, case of Amirun Nessa vs Golam Kashem reported in 42 DLR 499, case of Abdul Hamid vs Dr Sadeque Ali reported in 27 DLR 511, case of Abdul Quddus vs Anjuman Khatoon reported in 36 DLR 313, case of Abu Bakkar vs Nazir Ahmed reported in 34 DLR 239, case of Shaukat Ali vs Shamsum Bibi reported in 27 DLR 59. Mr Haque lastly submits that in the instant case the transaction i.e. the usufructuary mortgage began on 4-6-1966 and after 7 years on 4-6-1974 the term of usufructuary mortgage (খায় খালাসী বন্ধক) expired. So the transaction was alive when the President Order No. 88 of 1972 was promulgated. So the President Order No. 88 of 1972 and the provision of Section 95A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 are applicable on this transaction as it was alive up to 1974. So the President Order No. 88 of 1972 and provision of section 95A, the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950 should apply in this case and the Rule in the instant civil revision is liable to be discharged for end of justice with exemplary cost as the defendant deprived the plaintiff opposite party herein for a period of more then 4 decades. The defendant failed to prove his case by adducing oral and documentary evidence and the learned trial Court was unable to realize the legal issues involved in the suit as such committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice but the Appellate Court below rightly passed the judgment and decree on the basis of evidence and considering the legal issues.
